did.abstract: The Boston Seaman's Friend Society was formed December 13, 1827 out of Lyman Beecher's church on Hanover St in Boston, MA and was incorporated in 1829. The society was an independent branch of the American Seaman's Friend Society until 1888 when they turned to the New England Congregational churches and conferences for support. The BSFS started the Mariner's Church in 1830 and a boarding house that became the Sailors' Home in 1836. The Mariner's Church joined with the Salem St church to form the Salem and Mariner's Church in 1867 and moved to the corner of Salem and North Bennett streets where the Sailors' Home eventually shared space beginning in 1873 until the church closed in 1879 and the Home moved to Hanover St in 1893. A second branch on Martha's Vineyard was started in 1889 by chaplain Madison Edwards, and though there were periods of tension and decline, the branch continued until its close in 2003. The 1900s brought various changes including a reincorporation in 1922, renovations, two moves in the 1970s, changing relationships with other societies, the close of the Seaman's Congregational Church started in 1888, the start of two new branches in Portland, Maine and Portsmouth, New Hampshire in 1994, and a name change to Seafarer's Friend in 1998. The 2000s brought the permanent close of the boarding house, a move to Chelsea, Mass., the start of a branch in Searsport, Maine, additional office moves, and a continuation of the society's work as a maritime ministry working to meet the needs of seafarers. This collection contains records from the Boston Seaman's Friend Society and its branches including administrative records, property records, financial records, legal documents, reports, correspondence, histories, publications, house records, minutes, publicity, audiovisual material, ledgers and registers, plans, digital files, and other documents.

acqinfo.p: Materials were loaned to the Congregational Library & Archives by Boston Seaman's Friend Society in January 1988; accession number 1988-0. Additional materials were donated to the Congregational Library & Archives by Boston Seaman's Friend Society in October 2025; accession number 2025-22.

custodhist.head: Custodial History
custodhist.p: The Congregational Library and Archives collected material from the Boston Seaman's Friend Society, and about maritime ministry and history in Boston and New England. As part of an effort to standardize and ensure legal ownership and rights over their collections, the CLA asked for an agreement from BSFS to cover the materials they housed in 1987. In response, in January 1988, executive director Gene Landry on behalf of the BSFS placed the records on permanent loan or as a deposit in trust to the CLA. This collection, Boston Seaman's Friend Society records, 1827-1973, RG0776, was later processed in 1993 by Barbara Austen. As part of that processing, the five scrapbooks were microfilmed and added to their own collection, Boston Seaman's Friend Society records, 1827-1923, RG4681. In 1997, a researcher who had used some of the materials in the 1960s before the collection was processed, returned some annual reports and ephemera he had taken with him, and those were added to the existing RG0776 collection. In October 2025, a large accrual of records was donated from BSFS consisting of most of the society's records from its founding in 1827 until approximately 2020 which was added to the RG0776 collection. The collection was processed in 2026, and combined the original RG0776 collection, the microfilm reels of RG4681, and the new accrual to RG0776 into the current Boston Seaman's Friend Society, 1815-2021, RG0776 collection.

processinfo.p: This collection was processed by Madison Bellew, September 2026, according to the rules of Describing Archives: A Content Standard.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: The Boston Seaman's Friend Society was formed December 13, 1827 by a group of Congregationalists at Rev. Lyman Beeacher's church on Hanover Street in Boston, MA as an independent branch of the American Seaman's Friend Society that formed in New York a year previous. The origins and inspiration for the BSFS can be traced back to the Society for the Moral and Religious Instruction for the Poor and Rev. William Jenks' "Seamen's Meetings" under the Bethel flag on Central Wharf in the 1810s and 1820s. In 1828, the women of the society created the Ladies' Seaman's Friend Society as an auxiliary group to BSFS and in 1829, the BSFS was officially incorporated in Massachusetts. The society started the Mariner's Church in January 1830 with the dedication of the church building on Purchase St on the east side of Fort Hill where multiple services were held each Sunday and the Bethel flag welcomed both seamen and the local community. The 1830s also saw the opening of the Saving Bank for Seamen, eventually the Suffolk Franklin Savings Bank, in May 1833 through the collaboration of BSFS and the Boston Port Society, and the building of a wooden mansion on Purchase St in 1836 for use as a boarding house for seamen with rooms for rent, a library, and a reading room. In 1845, the boarding house or Sailors' Home was rebuilt as a brick structure through the combined efforts of the BSFS and the Ladies' Seaman's Friend Society. Unfortunately, fire destroyed both the Sailors' Home and the Mariner's Church on July 10, 1852, but the Home was quickly rebuilt at the same location and reopened March 1853 even larger than before while the church was moved to a new building on Summer and Sea Streets that was renovated and dedicated in December 1852. Shortly after in 1854, Rev. Elijah Kellogg took over as chaplain of the Mariner's Church and served until 1865. In 1867, the Mariner's Church combined with the Salem St church to become the Salem and Mariner's Church, and the building on Summer and Sea streets was sold so that the church could move to the building on the corner of Salem and North Bennett streets.

As Boston entered the 1870s, the city began leveling Fort Hill causing the Sailors' Home to close in 1872 and to sell the boarding house on Purchase St in March 1873. The church on Salem St was rebuilt that same year to accommodate both the Salem and Mariner's Church and the Sailors' Home in the same building. Unfortunately, due to changes in the city and movement of the population, the church congregation diminished until it decided to dissolve in 1879 and closed the Sailors' Home along with it. The society moved in 1880 to a hall at 175 Hanover St and sold the building on Salem St to the North Bennett School in 1884 after the school had been leasing the space since 1881. Eventually, the society purchased a building down the road at 287 Hanover St in 1892 and dedicated the space in January 1893 as the Sailor's Club House, where it also became known as "The Hook" for its anchor sign or the Sailor's Rest and Chapel.

The later decades of the 1800s and first half of the 1900s saw more changes than just the society's location. Some of the largest happened in 1888 with the dissolution of the relationship between BSFS and the American Seaman's Friend Society. The BSFS and ASFS had had a mutual financial relationship since 1846 and BSFS had been a branch of ASFS since its founding, but the Boston society chose to separate fully from the ASFS in 1888 and turn to the congregational churches of New England for support instead, though the two societies continued to collaborate for the benefit of seamen until ASFS's end in the 1970s. As they were now a fully independent society, the BSFS started their own newsletter, the "Sea Breeze", that year and also founded the Seaman's Congregational Church with chaplain Sylvester Nickerson, who began with BSFS in 1882 and served until 1903, as its pastor. Just a year later in 1889, a branch started in Martha's Vineyard through the work of chaplain Madison Edwards, and a year after that in 1890, Rev. Alexander McKenzie took over as president of BSFS until 1914. In 1895, Rev. McKenzie called on the women of the congregational churches and society to form the Women's Boston Seaman's Friend Society as an auxiliary group to BSFS which they remained until the societies separated in 1929. The BSFS and WBSFS later reaffiliated in 1942 to ensure the continuation of the women's work and support after a loss of funding and close of the women's "Hut" at the Chelsea Marine Hospital due to changing maritime needs in the wake of the world war. In 1902, a small boat was purchased to aid the society with visiting ships in Boston Harbor, and the Sailors' Home was renovated in 1910 to accommodate the numerous sailors visiting the society. In 1914, "Sailor Mother" Eleanor Roulston began the "Anchor Alliance" as a temperance society for seamen operating out of the Sailors' Home. August 1922 saw the society reincorporating as the Boston Seaman's Friend Society (Incorporated), and that year also saw the official endorsement of BSFS as an agent of the six New England Congregational Conferences even though collaboration and support had been coming from the conferences for some years before. In February 1938, the Seaman's Congregational Church formally closed after being inactive for some years though services and ministerial work continued to be done by the society's chaplains and chapel. As the society entered the 1940s, they saw more changes to their Home with their offices moving from 14 Beacon St to the Hanover St building in December 1942, the remodeling and rededication of 287 Hanover St in 1945, and the addition of the Scandinavian Sailor's Mission to the building in 1947 after the mission had lost their previous office space.

The next few decades brought various changes and trials for the BSFS legally, financially, and location wise. On July 20, 1960, the society again reincorporated and changed its name to Boston Seaman's Friend Society, Inc. The 1970s brought two separate moves for the Sailors' Home or Seaman's House as it was known by then. In 1970, the Hanover St property was sold and the society moved to 7 Park Sq, and then in 1978, the Park Sq building was claimed through eminent domain by the city of Boston for a redevelopment project in the area forcing a second move to 45 Church St even though operations continued at Park Sq until fall of 1979. The Seaman's House at Church St was dedicated and opened in 1981 after delays from renovations and zoning changes. Also occurring in the 1970s were splits between the BSFS, the WBSFS, and the Scandinavian Sailor's Mission. In 1972, the Scandinavian Sailor's Mission left the Park Sq house and the BSFS taking the chaplain Wallace Cedarleaf with them due to tensions over Cedarleaf's actions and intentions while serving both organizations. As part of this separation and tension along with other concerns about the treatment of their belongings and donations, the WBSFS also split from the BSFS in the same year. As a response, some of the women who chose not to leave the BSFS created the Women's Division of Boston Seaman's Friend Society in 1974 as an auxiliary group to BSFS. The 1980s followed these years of change with years of legal battles including an eminent domain case against the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for greater compensation for 7 Park Sq, a tax abatement case, a case against their neighbors Rifkin and later Emmer over use of the parking lot between the two buildings on Church St, various eviction cases for renters at the Seaman's House, and others.

The 1990s and into the 21st century saw the society adapting to the changes in the maritime industry and both an expansion and reduction of the BSFS. In 1994, branches in Portland, Maine and Portsmouth, New Hampshire were officially started though work had been done in years previous through local volunteers and churches. The Portland branch worked out of offices and a visitor center at the Portland Fish Pier at the Marine Trade Center starting in 1994 while Portsmouth was given space by the New Hampshire Public Services Company in 1998 for their offices and center. In 1997, the various maritime ministry organizations in New England came together to form the New England Maritime Ministries Association or NEMMA consisting of BSFS, the New England Seafarer's Mission which had previously been the Scandinavian Sailor's Mission, the Boston Port and Seaman's Aid Society which runs the Mariner's House, and the Apostleship of the Sea. The following year in March 1998, BSFS changed its name and logo to Seafarer's Friend in order to be more inclusive of those that they served while the legal corporate name remained the same. As costs rose, funding fell, and the time seafarers had in port decreased, the society chose to sell its building and discontinue the boarding house aspect of its ministry in 2000 with the Church St property fully closing in 2001. In 2002, offices were moved to Chelsea, MA to be closer to the ports with an additional move happening in 2005 from the first location on Williams St to a new office on Broadway St. The branches of the society also saw changes with the Martha's Vineyard branch fully closing in the early 2000s, and a new Searsport branch in Searsport, Maine operating out of the Portland office starting in 2008. Currently, Seafarer's Friend continues its work as a maritime ministry out of four branches across New England with Boston remaining its main office, working to aid, advocate for, and minister to the seafarers coming into the ports.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains records from, about, or related to the Boston Seaman's Friend Society and its branches in Maine, New Hampshire, and Martha's Vineyard, MA. The collection includes administrative, financial, legal, and property records along with annual reports, correspondence, histories, ship visit reports, policies, manuals, records and logs from the Seaman's House, inventories, financial and statistic reports, personnel and chaplain records and histories, records from their social welfare and ministerial work, and minutes and records from the various committees, board of directors, annual meeting and semi-annual meeting. Also included are records from, to, or about other organizations that the BSFS worked with, communicated with, or joined. The records contain cards, postcards, letters, flyers, brochures, pamphlets, booklets, scrapbooks, wooden and metal printing blocks, programs, newspapers, newsletters, photographs, photo slides, microfilm, CDs, VHS tapes, volumes and ledgers, deeds, maps, blueprints and plans, digital files, legal and court documents, reports, statements, and other related documents. Some gaps do exist in the collection, particularly for a few years of the house logs, as those along with other files remained in the care of the BSFS due to condition and preservation concerns.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This collection is arranged into seven series, four of which have subseries. Materials in this collection are arranged chronologically by start date.

phystech.head: Technical Requirements
phystech.p: A microfilm reader is required to access microform materials. One microfilm reader is available to the public upon request.
Various hardware is required to view audiovisual materials.

relatedmaterial.head: Related Materials
relatedmaterial.p: Additional records from the Mariner's Church and its successor the Salem and Mariner's Church can be found in Boston, Mass. Salem and Mariners' Church records, 1827-1879. RG1070. The museum collection and some of the associated records housed at the Bethel in Martha's Vineyard were moved to the Martha's Vineyard Museum. The Seaman's Bethel collection held by the museum includes print material from both the Boston Seaman's Friend Society and others interested in the Bethel. Records for other maritime ministry organizations are held by various institutions including the Records of the American Seamen's Friend Society at the G. W. Blunt White Library at the Mystic Seaport Museum, the Boston Port and Seamen's Aid Society records including records for Mariner's House at the Massachusetts Historical Society, and various items and publications at the Library of Congress.

odd.head: Content Warning
odd.p: This collection includes content and language that may be upsetting or triggering. These records reflect the language and attitudes of the historical period in which they were created; many of these terms are unacceptable today. The Congregational Library & Archives works to preserve Congregational history and stories while acknowledging that sometimes that history is problematic or questionable. We do this to preserve, contextualize, and reflect on the past so that we may learn from it.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series contains records from the Martha's Vineyard branch of the society located in the town of Tisbury, MA, also known as Vineyard Haven, on the island of Martha's Vineyard. The series contains records from or relating to the Seaman's Bethel, the Goldberg fund, chaplains Madison Edwards and Austin Tower, two seamen's cemetaries, and the maritime history of Vineyard Haven. The records include histories, correspondence, reports, financial records, property records, legal records, court documents, newspapers, personnel records, maps, blueprints and plans, inventories, and other related documents.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: In the later 1800s, the BSFS turned its eyes to the island of Martha's Vineyard and the seamen that visited, and the society hired Madison Edwards who had already been ministering to the seamen on his own to begin a branch on the island in 1888. When chaplain Edwards officially started in 1889, he ran three reading rooms in Tarpaulin Cove, Woods Hole, and Vineyard Haven, also known as the town of Tisbury, along with shipboard and shipside services for the sailors. In 1893, land was leased in Vineyard Haven at the end of the Steamship Wharf where a Seamen's Bethel with reading room and chapel was built to replace the previous reading room in a rented loft above a store near the water. That same year a boat was dedicated as the Helen May that Edwards used to bring seamen to shore to visit the Bethel and attend services. Due to the numerous sailors coming to the island at the time that created a need for both space for services and housing after shipwrecks, the Bethel was renovated in 1897 to enlarge the reading room and create an apartment for Edwards' family, and a building on the property was turned into a forecastle or dorm in 1899. Also in 1899, a burial lot, later known as the Bethel lot, was purchased in the Oak Grove cemetery in Tisbury so that Edwards could bury the sailors that died in shipwrecks or on the island instead of having to use the Marine Hospital cemetery, and in 1913, a lighthouse monument to honor those seamen was completed. In 1905, some of the buildings on the property including an old store were bought by the society and in 1906, a chaplain's office was added, and a new forecastle was built. In 1907, Edwards began the "Hold Fast" group as a form of Christian endeavor society for the sailors visiting the Bethel which later inspired Boston's "Anchor Alliance" endeavor. In 1921, the land the Bethel sat on was bought by the society instead of continuing to be leased, and when the society reincorporated in 1922, that property was transferred from the board to the BSFS. Chaplain Edwards died in 1926 and the work at the Seamen's Bethel was continued by his son-in-law Austin Tower who had been assisting Edwards since 1900. Tower continued as chaplain until his retirement in 1957 and as chaplain emeritus until his death in 1961, after which his daughter-in-law Teresa Tower cared for the Bethel until her retirement in 1981.

Over the course of the 1900s, the maritime industry on Martha's Vineyard changed and brought changes to the Bethel with it. In 1934, the reading room in Tarpaulin Cove closed due to lack of visitors, and only the Bethel remained as part of the Vineyard branch as the Woods Hole room had closed with the opening of the Bethel in 1893. In 1956, the society bought the Marine Hospital and its burial ground intending to sell the Bethel and move offices there to better accommodate their ministry. After the islanders' objections to the sale, the society chose to keep and renovate the Bethel and sold the Marine Hospital, except for the Sailor's Burial Ground, to the St. Pierre school in 1961. The Bethel was renovated and rededicated in 1965 with an added chapel in memorial for its two chaplains, and the reading room turned into museum space to house the items given to them over the years and to hopefully attract visitors. In 1973, the Bethel building and property was sold to the Steamship Authority which allowed the society to lease the Bethel and continue their ministry until 1991 when the society was evicted. The society moved offices in 1992 to Beach St., while the chapel building was moved to the Martha's Vineyard hospital, and the Bethel building was moved to the American Legion property in Vineyard Haven. In 1996, the society moved again and created the Vineyard Seafaring Center on Main St which they shared with Sail MV. The 1970s saw tensions between the society and the residents of Martha's Vineyard, partially due to the sale of the Bethel and partially due to the use of a bequest given to the society in 1954 for the maintenance of its Vineyard branch known as the Harriet Goldberg Fund. In 1975, the society petitioned the courts to allow the use of the Goldberg Fund for its general purposes, but a judgement in 1978 instructed the society to use the fund for the benefit of the island and its seamen. This was the first of many decisions, conversations, and legal intercessions involving the Goldberg fund, a similar bequest from Mary Marsh, the society, and the island residents which continued in varying levels of hostility until the society closed the Martha's Vineyard branch in 2003 due to a lack of visitors and purpose on the island. The society chose to transfer the Goldberg fund to the Permanent Endowment Fund of Martha's Vineyard in 2006 to be used as scholarships and grants for island residents and seafarers. The close of the branch also necessitated the transfer of the Sailor's Burial Ground and its upkeep to the Martha's Vineyard Land Bank in 2006 with the Bethel lot already being cared for by the town of Tisbury, and the donation of the Bethel museum collection to the Martha's Vineyard Historical Society in 2006 except for a few items given to the American Legion and those kept by the society.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series contains records from or related to other organizations and groups that BSFS interacted, collaborated, or corresponded with. These organizations included regional, national, and international associations of maritime ministries or the maritime industry along with independent organizations who had connections to the maritime industry, the congregationalists, or social welfare. Also included in this series are the records from the women's division of the BSFS which was a subordinate group within BSFS and a separate organization from the Women's Seafarer's Friend Society, whose records are included as well. The records contain correspondence, programs, addresses, extracts, histories, meetings, directories, and other material.

scopecontent.p: This series contains records from the society's history, ministerial and social work, ship visiting, chaplains, volunteers, events, and efforts as a Christian mission society. The records contain pamphlets, booklets, brochures, articles, newspapers, newsletters, publications, histories, programs, ship visit reports, personnel histories and records, correspondence, anniversaries, historical research, historical records, and other related records.
